h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: At high learning rates many runs are diverged or near chance, so alpha's usual harm is compressed toward zero and L2 may even help by bounding weight growth.
Under standard parameterisation the function-space change per Adam step grows with fan-in, so widening pushes an already-large learning rate past stability.
High-variance tiny-batch gradients compound through an extra layer, destabilising deeper nets more than shallow ones.
Strong L2 shrinks every weight matrix, so an extra layer multiplies another shrunken factor into the end-to-end map and deepens underfitting.
With a tiny learning rate the net is already undertrained in 243 epochs, so cutting the number of updates via a larger batch hurts much more.
Large batches give few, low-variance updates, so a larger learning rate restores progress without the instability it causes at small batch.
In a one-hidden-layer net width is the only route to capacity, whereas deeper nets already get capacity from depth, so extra width matters more when shallow.
In sklearn MLPs the L2 gradient is divided by the batch size and applied fewer times per epoch, so large batches dilute the extra penalty.
When strong L2 forces underfitting, extra units restore capacity the penalty removed, so widening helps more under heavy regularisation.
At large learning rates deeper nets diverge or suffer dead-ReLU collapse sooner, so adding a layer is more harmful there.
